segments.voice: Yesterday, in Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum, lesson one: the sankalpa, a resolve made in daylight with water in the palm. Today closes the week.
screen: `THE SANKALPA, MADE IN DAYLIGHT.` · `THE WEEK CLOSES.`

segments.voice: On the day of Shivaratri, in some kitchens, the stove is still on. The food has just changed. No rice, no wheat, no lentils. Instead, sago pearls softening with potato and crushed peanuts, a bowl of fruit, a glass of milk. In other homes nothing goes on the stove, and people take only water until the next morning. Different vows, different tables. But in each, the stomach speaks up, in the afternoon, the evening, around midnight. Today's lesson is what to do when it rings.
screen: `THE KITCHEN CHANGES.` → `DIFFERENT VOWS, DIFFERENT TABLES.` → `THE STOMACH SPEAKS UP.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word for a fast is upavasa. Some teachers hear in it the sense of staying near, and read the fast that way: not going without, but keeping close to the one the night is for. Look at what a fast does on this night. First, it clears space. No meals to cook, serve and clean up means hours handed back, and the vow spends them on worship. Second, it turns hunger into a bell. Each pang can be met with one question: why am I awake? The ringing keeps calling the mind home. Third, a fast is held inside a vow, not a punishment. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says yoga isn't for the one who eats too much, nor for the one who doesn't eat at all. So a household keeping Shivaratri can make room for children, for the sick, and for anyone a fast would hurt. A glass of milk taken honestly under the vow is still the vow. Now look back at the week. The Rudram bowed to the short and the tall, to trees and foam, then asked, and to me, and we left it chanted as water poured over the stone. Then the night opened: its shape, the morning resolve, and now the fast. A fierce thing, met with a bow. A long night, met with a promise. Hunger, met with a question. Each time, something hard is turned into attention.
screen: `UPAVASA: STAYING NEAR.` · `A FAST CLEARS SPACE.` · `HUNGER BECOMES A BELL.` · `NOT TOO MUCH, NOT NONE AT ALL.` · then, large: `THE HARD THING BECOMES ATTENTION.`

segments.voice: Sooner or later something will tug at you, an itch, a thought of food, the urge to check a message; don't act on it or fight it, just ask quietly, why am I sitting here, and come back to the breath. Each tug is one more ring of the bell, and one more return. If you pray, you can let each return carry Shiva's name, or the name of God you use.
Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. Lesson two: upavasa, the fast, which clears space and turns every pang of hunger into a bell that calls you back.
Your line: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. Hunger can be a bell. That's the week.

howItsDone: Hindus who fast on Maha Shivaratri keep different vows: some take only water, some take fruit, milk and special fasting foods such as sago, and the fast is usually broken the next morning after worship.
